6511:
In BALLY Basic TXTUNF is at $4E52 or since my notes are in decimal:
"Print %(20050)" should print "-24572" with no program loaded, and
@(1) should also be at the same address as %(-24572) WHEN NO PROGRAM
IS LOADED.  It will bump up as your program is entered.  "Print SZ"
returns a function of -22772 - %(20050) which is 1800 bytes or less.

In ASTRO Basic TXTUNF is at $4E20 or 20000, and the TEXT Area is at
the same software map of -24576 up to -22777 ($A000 to $A707) - not
actual addresses since that is in extended memory range, of course.

I would imagine you could set up a display list using the
interrupt line port. You have a list where each entry will
describe each line of the screen. It's not a TRUE display
list in hardware like the Atari's have but it can act like
the same thing. I know you are using a basic, however if
Color Basic already makes use of the interrupt line, you
may not be able to do it. that will depend on Just how much
use it makes of the interrupt line....but in case its ok to
do so...

....if I remember this correctly......

Essentially you need to set your interrupt line which when
being drawn, will generate an interrupt when it is finished
drawing that line(this is a horizontal interrupt, generated
for each of the 102 lines of the display.)

So you have a few cycles to do a few things there.

How many exactly but what you need to do is have a look up table,
or display list data for each line you decide to change colors on.

In this blanking period you should

A ) Update the interrupt line value
B ) Update the color register(s)
C ) Update the pointer to the next line

An entry in your list should look something
like this

WHITE   .EQU   $07
RED     .EQU   $48
GREEN   .EQU   $AA
BLUE    .EQU   $08

DISPLAY_LIST:
     .DB WHITE, 1
     .DB RED, 25
     .DB GREEN, 50
     .DB BLUE, 75
     .DB 0,0

As you see above, you do not have to do this every line.

Use the 0,0 to let you know you are at the end of screen
list and reset your pointer to 'DISPLAY_LIST' in the vertical
blank.

You obviously need to know assembler for this one and it would
require you to either hook into an already employed list or at
the begining of your COLOR BASIC program, set up the interrupts
IF, it will allow you to.

There is no such thing as a high res Astrocade console.Not
unless you are willing to hack the unit and add the other 3
banks of video RAM(which is also usable as plain old system
RAM, but hook up directly to the DATA and the ADDRESS chip).

The Astrocade chip set is actually capable of THREE modes
of operation according to my ancient talks with Bob Ogdon.
(Someone that would be great to see pop in here from time
to time.)

You have the following modes

160 x 102 Low Res
160 x 204 medium Res
320 x 204 High Res

The astrocade HVGS console can only do low res due to the
lack of RAM or the ability to easily expand the current RAM.

However...

There are tricks you can play with the system to get 160x102
but it only occupies the upper left quadrant of the screen.

Essentially its the same res in a smaller window. The idea
(I believe) was to show you what high res pixels from the
Astrocade Console would look like. I think it was a type in
from the Arcadian if I am not mistaken.

The two biggest mistakes in the astrocade design is the lack
of the proper signals to expand the video and the lack of a
hardware assited drawing apparatis.

The Arcade Astrocade units in some of the games actually use
what is known as a pattern board. These are found in the rack
cage version of the hardware, Gorf, Robby Roto, Wizrad of Wor
and Space Zap. It is essentially a bare bones blitter. This
way the Z-80 can compute and the pattern board can draw,
allowing for more objects on screen.

Keep in mind folks, The astrocade console is slow at drawing
for many reasons. If the unit was high The Z-80 is quite a
cycle hog. The instruction set with all its blessings is cursed
with a few missing instructions.....for instance LD r,(IX+A)
would have been an enormous help. The Jaguar RISC's have pretty
much spoiled me I guess. :D

RAM, a simple GPU of some sort and maybe even RS-232.

shows the background changing to mark each of the three parts [oh, yeah
- if using MESS then turn off FRAMESKIP or else it will not show all of
the color bars correctly.] - in RED starting with the screen interrupt
at scanline #127 down to line #145 is the time it takes to do the
VECT[or] system routine (a little longer when Ziggy hits the side and
more math has to be done.)
If only a small fractional change is made and the image doesn't need to
be redrawn then the background changes back to WHITE and the interrupt
is over (about 1.17 microSecond out of the 16.67uS per each 1/60th
Second screen if my math is right.)  But ...
If it DOES need to re-draw first it has to un-draw.  From line #145 all
the way to #209 the screen is GREEN while the VBLANK system routine
erases the old image.  This takes 3.84uS due to the size of the image
plus the column of bytes to the right that it might have been shifted
into.
By now the bottom of the screen has been passed so you won't see the
change to BLUE at line #209 but it wraps around to the top and down to
line #24 while the VWRITR (Vector WRITe Relative) routine expands the
image to the screen, another 4.95uS passes for a total of 153 scanlines,
at almost 10uS, when the background turns WHITE again, the HALT is over,
and game code runs again.

Since there are only 103 scanlines, or about 6.71uS (and yes, there is
supposed to be a tail on that 'u' for micro), left for the game code to
finish and get back to the EI/HLT combo - there is not enough time for
to add in another image/player UNLESS they redraw on alternate screens.
